items.article_text_original: Biological products include a wide range of products such as vaccines, blood and blood components, allergenics, somatic cells, gene therapy, tissues, and recombinant therapeutic proteins. The Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) is responsible for ensuring the safety and efficacy of the biological products. An Investigational New Drug Application (IND) is a request for authorization from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to administer an investigational drug or biological product to humans. Such authorization must be secured prior to interstate shipment and administration of any new drug or biological product that is not the subject of an approved New Drug Application or Biologics/Product License Application. In rare instances a physician may request an Emergency Use IND for a patient. Contact information for Emergency Use IND Requests: - For investigational biological products regulated by CBER, call 240-402-7800 - For all other investigational drugs, call 301-796-3400 or 1-855-543-3784 - After working hours, call FDA's Office of Emergency Operations at 301-796-8240 Paragraph Header Contact Us White Oak Campus 10903 New Hampshire Ave Silver Spring, MD 20993 United States

items.article_text_original: Vaccines, as with all products regulated by FDA, undergo a rigorous review of laboratory and clinical data to ensure the safety, efficacy, purity and potency of these products. Vaccines approved for marketing may also be required to undergo additional studies to further evaluate the vaccine and often to address specific questions about the vaccine's safety, effectiveness or possible side effects. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, vaccines have reduced preventable infectious diseases to an all-time low and now few people experience the devastating effects of measles, pertussis and other illnesses. The Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) regulates vaccine products. Many of these are childhood vaccines that have contributed to a significant reduction of vaccine-preventable diseases. items.summary_ai_original: Rio de Janeiro, September 3, 2026 (PANAFTOSA/VPH-PAHO/WHO) – The Pan American Center for Foot-and-Mouth Disease and Veterinary Public Health (PANAFTOSA) of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has launched the Methodology for Estimating Dog and Cat Populations in Latin America and the Caribbean, a new tool desig
items.article_text_original: The methodology provides a practical and adaptable approach to estimating dog and cat populations, improving the planning of vaccination campaigns, disease surveillance, and other public health interventions. Rio de Janeiro, September 3, 2026 (PANAFTOSA/VPH-PAHO/WHO) – The Pan American Center for Foot-and-Mouth Disease and Veterinary Public Health (PANAFTOSA) of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has launched the Methodology for Estimating Dog and Cat Populations in Latin America and the Caribbean, a new tool designed to help countries generate more reliable data on dog and cat populations and strengthen the planning of public health and animal health interventions. “Understanding the size, distribution, and characteristics of dog and cat populations is essential for guiding public health and animal health actions,” said Manuel Sánchez Vázquez, Director of PANAFTOSA. “This methodology provides countries with a practical tool to generate reliable information, strengthen the prevention of zoonotic diseases, and support evidence-based decision-making through a One Health approach.” The relationship between people and dogs and cats brings important benefits, ranging from companionship and emotional well-being to support in activities such as guarding, herding, pest control, and assistance for people with disabilities. However, irresponsible ownership, abandonment, and uncontrolled breeding can contribute to the presence of free-roaming animals and create challenges for public health. Close interaction between people, dogs, and cats can also facilitate the transmission of zoonotic diseases, including rabies, sporotrichosis, dermatophytosis, Bartonella henselae infection, visceral leishmaniasis, and echinococcosis. Although countries in the Americas have made significant progress in preventing and controlling dog-mediated rabies, the disease continues to claim lives in the Region. Between 2023 and August 2026, 62 human rabies cases were reported in the Americas, including 32 associated with dog transmission. Each year, countries across the Region vaccinate at least 50 million dogs through public vaccination campaigns as part of efforts to prevent rabies transmission and protect both human and animal health. Sustaining and expanding these gains requires up-to-date information on animal populations and the areas where risks remain highest. An adaptable methodology for different settings Dog and cat populations vary depending on their relationship with people. In urban areas, for example, owned, semi-owned, community, and free-roaming animals may coexist. Understanding how these populations are distributed helps authorities design more effective interventions tailored to local realities. To address this challenge, the methodology offers a standardized yet flexible approach that can be adapted to different geographic and social contexts while generating reliable population estimates for decision-making. The methodology includes practical implementation tools such as adaptable questionnaires, fieldwork checklists, and guidance for data analysis. The approach allows data collection to be tailored to the demographic, geographic, and social characteristics of each locality. Information generated through the methodology can help public health and animal health authorities identify risks, design interventions tailored to local needs and strengthen the prevention and response to zoonotic diseases. The publication is intended to support public health and animal health authorities in generating dog and cat population estimates to strengthen zoonotic disease surveillance and control, improve planning for rabies vaccination campaigns, and support other public health actions.

items.summary_original: Patient factsheet providing information on influenza (flu) and flu vaccination.
items.summary_ai_original: This means that each year, to prepare for the upcoming flu season, scientists across the world collect and look at information about which new flu viruses are emerging. This factsheet covers: - Overview of flu - Flu vaccination and eligibility - How flu vaccines work - Types of flu vaccines - Flu vaccines and pregnancy
items.article_text_original: Influenza (flu) is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses that spread easily through coughs, sneezes, and close contact. Flu can cause sudden fever, tiredness, aches and pains, and difficulty breathing. Many people recover within a week, but flu can sometimes lead to serious illness and complications, especially in young children, older adults, pregnant individuals, and people with long-term health conditions. Influenza is seasonal, which means you are more likely to catch it in winter. Unlike some viruses, the influenza viruses are constantly changing. This means that each year, to prepare for the upcoming flu season, scientists across the world collect and look at information about which new flu viruses are emerging. Seasonal flu vaccines are therefore updated each year to match the strains of the virus that are expected to circulate. Vaccination is one of the safest and most effective ways to help reduce the chance of getting flu and to lower the risk of serious illness if you do catch it. Influenza vaccines used in the UK have been rigorously assessed for safety, quality and effectiveness, and continue to be monitored, including through the Yellow Card scheme. This factsheet covers: - Overview of flu - Flu vaccination and eligibility - How flu vaccines work - Types of flu vaccines - Flu vaccines and pregnancy - Safety and effectiveness of flu vaccines - How flu vaccines are updated - Who should not receive the flu vaccine - Flu vaccine side effects - Less common side effects - Report side effects to the Yellow Card scheme
